doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

title: Critics who ignore early jazz; was jazz always an art form
summary: Yanow likes hearing how jazz evolved and says most critics skip pre-Parker music; he thinks the art form label is overdone though early jazz was artistic.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: But you know it’s just the basic idea I liked to hear how it all evolved and how it all connects together. And because I was lucky enough to start with Dixieland and the 1920s jazz, I still love listening to that today, where most critics and jazz journalists, they don’t go further back from Charlie Parker, usually. You know you have Benny Goodman and Duke Ellington, but they’re not really going to go back to the earliest music because the recording quality doesn’t agree with them and it seems too simple. They don’t quite understand or appreciate how it all connects together.
Do you feel that there’s a determination on their part that that music wasn’t really an art form or worthy of being an art form, thus worthy of critiquing?

Well I always thought the art form connection to jazz was kind of overdone to tell you the truth. Now of course it was an art form from the very beginning. I mean Buddy Bolden most likely played music that could be considered artistic, and certainly by the time recordings were made of the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, I mean it’s way ahead of its time, you know, compared to most of the music that was recorded. Most of the music from 1917 or so that’s on records is really unlistenable at this point, you know because it’s just too primitive or it’s just very predictable. But jazz still sounds fresh, even if it’s over 100 years old, if it’s well played you know.
